questions.q:
An aqueous solution of a lead(II) salt is divided into two test tubes. Addition of potassium iodide to the first test tube produces a yellow precipitate 'X' which dissolves in boiling water and recrystallizes on cooling. Addition of potassium chromate to the second test tube produces a yellow precipitate 'Y' which is insoluble in acetic acid.

The chemical identities of precipitates X and Y respectively are:
questions.question:
An aqueous solution of a lead(II) salt is divided into two test tubes. Addition of potassium iodide to the first test tube produces a yellow precipitate 'X' which dissolves in boiling water and recrystallizes on cooling. Addition of potassium chromate to the second test tube produces a yellow precipitate 'Y' which is insoluble in acetic acid.

The chemical identities of precipitates X and Y respectively are:
questions.solution:
The reaction of $Pb^{2+}$ with $KI$ yields a yellow precipitate of lead iodide ($PbI_2$). A unique characteristic of $PbI_2$ is that it dissolves in boiling water to give a colorless solution and recrystallizes as golden spangles upon cooling.

The reaction of $Pb^{2+}$ with $K_2CrO_4$ yields a yellow precipitate of lead chromate ($PbCrO_4$), which is insoluble in acetic acid but soluble in sodium hydroxide.

Thus, X is $PbI_2$ and Y is $PbCrO_4$.

Answer: X = $PbI_2$, Y = $PbCrO_4$

The white precipitate is filtered and dissolved in dilute acetic acid. When aqueous potassium chromate ($\text{K}_2\text{CrO}_4$) is added to this acidic solution, a yellow precipitate is formed. Identify the cation present in the salt.
questions.question: An inorganic salt solution gives a white precipitate when treated with $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{CO}_3$ in the presence of $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ and $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$. The white precipitate is filtered and dissolved in dilute acetic acid. When aqueous potassium chromate ($\text{K}_2\text{CrO}_4$) is added to this acidic solution, a yellow precipitate is formed. Identify the cation present in the salt.
questions.solution:
The formation of a white precipitate upon the addition of $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{CO}_3$ in the presence of $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ and $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ indicates the presence of a Group V cation ($\text{Ba}^{2+}$, $\text{Sr}^{2+}$, or $\text{Ca}^{2+}$).

The white precipitate is the metal carbonate ($\text{MCO}_3$), which dissolves in dilute acetic acid to form the corresponding soluble metal acetate.

Among the Group V cations, only $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ forms a yellow precipitate of barium chromate ($\text{BaCrO}_4$) upon the addition of aqueous $\text{K}_2\text{CrO}_4$.

$\text{Sr}^{2+}$ and $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ do not precipitate with chromate under these conditions. Although $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ also forms a yellow chromate precipitate, it belongs to Group I/II and its initial precipitation behavior does not match the Group V scheme. Thus, the cation is $\text{Ba}^{2+}$.

Answer: $\text{Ba}^{2+}$

An aqueous solution containing $Pb^{2+}$ ions reacts with $K_2CrO_4$ to yield a yellow precipitate (A). When precipitate (A) is treated with hot concentrated $NaOH$, it dissolves to form a clear solution containing a soluble complex (B).

The chemical formula of the soluble complex (B) is:
questions.question:
An aqueous solution containing $Pb^{2+}$ ions reacts with $K_2CrO_4$ to yield a yellow precipitate (A). When precipitate (A) is treated with hot concentrated $NaOH$, it dissolves to form a clear solution containing a soluble complex (B).

The chemical formula of the soluble complex (B) is:
questions.solution:
When potassium chromate is added to a solution containing $Pb^{2+}$ ions, a yellow precipitate of lead chromate (A) is formed.

$Pb^{2+} + CrO_4^{2-} \rightarrow PbCrO_4 \downarrow$

Lead is an amphoteric metal, and its salts like lead chromate dissolve in excess of strong alkalis such as sodium hydroxide. The dissolution occurs due to the formation of a soluble tetrahydroxoplumbate(II) complex (B).

$PbCrO_4 + 4NaOH \rightarrow Na_2[Pb(OH)_4] + Na_2CrO_4$

Thus, the soluble complex (B) is $Na_2[Pb(OH)_4]$.

Answer: $Na_2[Pb(OH)_4]$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
An unknown transition metal salt $X$ is subjected to the borax bead test. It forms a transparent blue bead when heated in an oxidizing flame and allowed to cool. When the same bead is heated in a reducing flame and cooled, it turns opaque red.

The spin-only magnetic moment of the metal cation responsible for the blue colour in the oxidizing flame is closest to:
questions.question:
An unknown transition metal salt $X$ is subjected to the borax bead test. It forms a transparent blue bead when heated in an oxidizing flame and allowed to cool. When the same bead is heated in a reducing flame and cooled, it turns opaque red.

The spin-only magnetic moment of the metal cation responsible for the blue colour in the oxidizing flame is closest to:
questions.solution:
The characteristic colour changes in the borax bead test identify the metal present in salt $X$.

A blue bead in an oxidizing flame (when cold) that turns opaque red in a reducing flame (when cold) is characteristic of copper.

In the oxidizing flame, copper forms copper(II) metaborate, $\text{Cu}(\text{BO}_2)_2$. The metal cation responsible for the blue colour is $\text{Cu}^{2+}$.

The atomic number of copper is $29$. Its electronic configuration is $[\text{Ar}] 3d^{10} 4s^1$.
For the $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ion, the electronic configuration is $[\text{Ar}] 3d^9$.

In the $3d^9$ configuration, there is $1$ unpaired electron ($n = 1$).

The spin-only magnetic moment $\mu$ is given by the formula:
$\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} \text{ BM}$
$\mu = \sqrt{1(1+2)} = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.73 \text{ BM}$

Answer: $1.73 \text{ BM}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An inorganic salt containing sulphur gives a characteristic purple colouration when its sodium carbonate extract is treated with sodium nitroprusside. The oxidation state of the central metal atom in the newly formed purple complex is :
questions.question: An inorganic salt containing sulphur gives a characteristic purple colouration when its sodium carbonate extract is treated with sodium nitroprusside. The oxidation state of the central metal atom in the newly formed purple complex is :
questions.solution:
The reaction of sulphide ions with sodium nitroprusside yields a purple coloured complex, $\mathrm{Na}_4\left[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_5 \mathrm{NOS}\right]$.

The complex ion is $\left[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_5 \mathrm{NOS}\right]^{4-}$.

In this complex, the ligands are five cyanide ions ($\mathrm{CN}^{-}$) and one $\mathrm{NOS}^{-}$ ion. The $\mathrm{NOS}^{-}$ ligand is formed by the attack of $\mathrm{S}^{2-}$ on the $\mathrm{NO}^{+}$ ligand of the original nitroprusside complex, resulting in a net charge of $-1$ for the $\mathrm{NOS}$ group.

Let the oxidation state of iron ($\mathrm{Fe}$) be $x$.
The sum of oxidation states is equal to the net charge on the complex ion:
$x + 5(-1) + 1(-1) = -4$
$x - 6 = -4$
$x = +2$

Therefore, the oxidation state of the central metal atom is $+2$.

Answer: $+2$

questions.q: An aqueous solution of an unknown metal salt is subjected to qualitative analysis. When $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ gas is passed through the solution in the presence of dilute $\text{HCl}$, no precipitate is observed. However, when $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ gas is passed through the same solution after making it alkaline with $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ in the presence of $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$, a distinct precipitate is formed. The metal cation present in the solution is:
questions.question: An aqueous solution of an unknown metal salt is subjected to qualitative analysis. When $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ gas is passed through the solution in the presence of dilute $\text{HCl}$, no precipitate is observed. However, when $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ gas is passed through the same solution after making it alkaline with $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ in the presence of $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$, a distinct precipitate is formed. The metal cation present in the solution is:
questions.solution:
The qualitative analysis of cations relies on selective precipitation based on solubility products. Group II cations (such as $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ and $\text{Pb}^{2+}$) precipitate as sulphides when $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ is passed in an acidic medium. Since no precipitate is formed in the acidic medium, Group II cations are absent.

Group IV cations (such as $\text{Co}^{2+}$, $\text{Ni}^{2+}$, $\text{Mn}^{2+}$, and $\text{Zn}^{2+}$) require a higher concentration of sulphide ions to precipitate. This is achieved by passing $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ in an alkaline medium (using $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ and $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$). Since a precipitate forms under these conditions, the cation belongs to Group IV.

Among the given options, $\text{Co}^{2+}$ is a Group IV cation. $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ belongs to Group V and does not precipitate as a sulphide in either medium.

Answer: $\text{Co}^{2+}$

questions.q: When ammonia gas is passed through an alkaline solution of potassium tetraiodomercurate(II), a precipitate is formed. The colour and the chemical formula of this precipitate are respectively:
questions.question: When ammonia gas is passed through an alkaline solution of potassium tetraiodomercurate(II), a precipitate is formed. The colour and the chemical formula of this precipitate are respectively:
questions.solution:
An alkaline solution of potassium tetraiodomercurate(II) ($\mathrm{K}_2[\mathrm{HgI}_4] + \mathrm{KOH}$) is known as Nessler's reagent.

When ammonia gas is passed through Nessler's reagent, it reacts to form a brown precipitate of the iodide of Millon's base.

The chemical reaction is given by:
$2\mathrm{K}_2[\mathrm{HgI}_4] + \mathrm{NH}_3 + 3\mathrm{KOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{HgO} \cdot \mathrm{Hg}(\mathrm{NH}_2)\mathrm{I} \downarrow + 7\mathrm{KI} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}$

Thus, the precipitate is brown in colour and its chemical formula is $\mathrm{HgO} \cdot \mathrm{Hg}(\mathrm{NH}_2)\mathrm{I}$.

Answer: Brown, $\mathrm{HgO} \cdot \mathrm{Hg}(\mathrm{NH}_2)\mathrm{I}$

questions.q: A Group IV transition metal cation $\text{M}^{2+}$ reacts with dimethylglyoxime in an ammoniacal medium to yield a brilliant red precipitate of a complex. The hybridization and the magnetic nature of the central metal atom in this complex are respectively:
questions.question: A Group IV transition metal cation $\text{M}^{2+}$ reacts with dimethylglyoxime in an ammoniacal medium to yield a brilliant red precipitate of a complex. The hybridization and the magnetic nature of the central metal atom in this complex are respectively:
questions.solution:
The formation of a brilliant red precipitate with dimethylglyoxime (DMG) in an ammoniacal medium indicates that the metal cation $\text{M}^{2+}$ is $\text{Ni}^{2+}$. The complex formed is bis(dimethylglyoximato)nickel(II), $[\text{Ni}(\text{DMG})_2]$.

In this complex, Nickel is in a $+2$ oxidation state with a $3\text{d}^{8}$ electronic configuration.

Although DMG is generally a weak field ligand, in this specific complex it acts as a strong field ligand due to the extra stability provided by intramolecular hydrogen bonding between the two DMG ligands. This causes the pairing of the two unpaired $3\text{d}$ electrons, leaving one inner $3\text{d}$ orbital empty.

The empty $3\text{d}$, one $4\text{s}$, and two $4\text{p}$ orbitals undergo $\text{dsp}^{2}$ hybridization to form a square planar complex. Since all electrons are paired, the complex is diamagnetic.

Answer: $\text{dsp}^{2}$, diamagnetic

questions.question:

questions.solution:
When aqueous solutions of metal cations react with potassium ferrocyanide, $\mathrm{K}_4[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6]$:

(A) $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$ reacts to form a chocolate brown precipitate of cupric ferrocyanide, $\mathrm{Cu}_2[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6]$.

(B) $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ reacts to form a Prussian blue precipitate of ferric ferrocyanide, $\mathrm{Fe}_4[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6]_3$.

(C) $\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}$ reacts to form a white or bluish-white precipitate of $\mathrm{K}_2\mathrm{Zn}_3[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6]_2$.

(D) $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ reacts to form a white precipitate of Everitt's salt, $\mathrm{K}_2\mathrm{Fe}[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6]$, which rapidly oxidizes in air to form Prussian blue.

Therefore, the correct matching is (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV).

Answer: (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A student is given an aqueous mixture containing $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ and $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$ ions. Upon adding solid $\mathrm{NH_4Cl}$ followed by excess $\mathrm{NH_4OH}$ solution, a brown precipitate forms, but $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$ remains in the solution. The combined thermodynamic and equilibrium reason why $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$ does not precipitate under these specific conditions is that :
questions.question: A student is given an aqueous mixture containing $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ and $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$ ions. Upon adding solid $\mathrm{NH_4Cl}$ followed by excess $\mathrm{NH_4OH}$ solution, a brown precipitate forms, but $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$ remains in the solution. The combined thermodynamic and equilibrium reason why $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$ does not precipitate under these specific conditions is that :
options: the common ion effect of $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$ keeps $[\mathrm{OH}^{-}]$ low, which fails to exceed the higher $K_{\mathrm{sp}}$ of $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$
$\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$ has a lower $K_{\mathrm{sp}}$ than $\mathrm{Fe(OH)_3}$, preventing its precipitation in basic medium
the common ion effect of $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$ suppresses the dissociation of the mixture, preventing the precipitation of $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$
$\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$ forms a highly soluble ammine complex $[\mathrm{Mg(NH_3)_4}]^{2+}$ with excess ammonia
questions.solution:
Ammonium hydroxide ($\mathrm{NH_4OH}$) is a weak base, and its ionization is suppressed by the addition of the strong electrolyte ammonium chloride ($\mathrm{NH_4Cl}$) due to the common ion effect of $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$ ions.

$\mathrm{NH_4OH} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{NH_4^+} + \mathrm{OH}^{-}$
$\mathrm{NH_4Cl} \rightarrow \mathrm{NH_4^+} + \mathrm{Cl}^{-}$

This suppression keeps the concentration of $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ ions very low in the solution. The solubility product ($K_{\mathrm{sp}}$) of $\mathrm{Fe(OH)_3}$ is much lower (around $10^{-38}$) compared to that of $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$ (around $10^{-11}$). The low $[\mathrm{OH}^{-}]$ is sufficient to make the ionic product of $\mathrm{Fe(OH)_3}$ exceed its $K_{\mathrm{sp}}$, leading to its precipitation. However, the ionic product of $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$ does not exceed its relatively higher $K_{\mathrm{sp}}$, so $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$ remains dissolved in the solution.

Answer: the common ion effect of $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$ keeps $[\mathrm{OH}^{-}]$ low, which fails to exceed the higher $K_{\mathrm{sp}}$ of $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$

Ammonium hydroxide ($\mathrm{NH_4OH}$) is a weak base, and its ionization is suppressed by the addition of the strong electrolyte ammonium chloride ($\mathrm{NH_4Cl}$) due to the common ion effect of $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$ ions.

$\mathrm{NH_4OH} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{NH_4^+} + \mathrm{OH}^{-}$
$\mathrm{NH_4Cl} \rightarrow \mathrm{NH_4^+} + \mathrm{Cl}^{-}$

This suppression keeps the concentration of $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ ions very low in the solution. The solubility product ($K_{\mathrm{sp}}$) of $\mathrm{Fe(OH)_3}$ is much lower (around $10^{-38}$) compared to that of $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$ (around $10^{-11}$). Answer: the common ion effect of $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$ keeps $[\mathrm{OH}^{-}]$ low, which fails to exceed the higher $K_{\mathrm{sp}}$ of $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$

questions.question: An aqueous solution of a salt containing a cation $Z^{n+}$ reacts with potassium hexacyanoferrate(II) solution to yield a characteristic Prussian blue precipitate. The identity of the cation $Z^{n+}$ and the chemical formula of the Prussian blue precipitate are respectively:
questions.solution:
In the qualitative analysis of Group III cations, the $Fe^{3+}$ ion reacts with potassium hexacyanoferrate(II), $K_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}]$, to form a characteristic Prussian blue precipitate.

The chemical reaction is given by:
$4Fe^{3+} + 3K_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}] \rightarrow Fe_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}]_{3} \downarrow + 12K^{+}$

The Prussian blue precipitate is Iron(III) hexacyanoferrate(II), which has the formula $Fe_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}]_{3}$.

Answer: $Fe^{3+}$ and $Fe_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}]_{3}$
questions.explanation:
In the qualitative analysis of Group III cations, the $Fe^{3+}$ ion reacts with potassium hexacyanoferrate(II), $K_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}]$, to form a characteristic Prussian blue precipitate.

The chemical reaction is given by:
$4Fe^{3+} + 3K_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}] \rightarrow Fe_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}]_{3} \downarrow + 12K^{+}$

The Prussian blue precipitate is Iron(III) hexacyanoferrate(II), which has the formula $Fe_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}]_{3}$.

Answer: $Fe^{3+}$ and $Fe_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}]_{3}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An aqueous solution of an unknown inorganic salt is treated with solid $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ and an aqueous solution of $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$. Upon subsequent addition of an aqueous solution of $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{CO}_3$, a white precipitate is formed. Which of the following cations is most likely present in the solution?
questions.question: An aqueous solution of an unknown inorganic salt is treated with solid $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ and an aqueous solution of $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$. Upon subsequent addition of an aqueous solution of $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{CO}_3$, a white precipitate is formed. Which of the following cations is most likely present in the solution?
questions.solution:
The reagent mixture of $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$, $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$, and $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{CO}_3$ is the group reagent for Group V cations in systematic qualitative analysis.

The Group V cations include $\text{Ba}^{2+}$, $\text{Sr}^{2+}$, and $\text{Ca}^{2+}$. They precipitate as their respective insoluble carbonates (e.g., $\text{SrCO}_3$).

$\text{Mg}^{2+}$ belongs to Group VI and does not precipitate here because the presence of $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ suppresses the ionization of $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{CO}_3$, keeping the carbonate ion concentration too low to exceed the solubility product of $\text{MgCO}_3$.

$\text{Zn}^{2+}$ (Group IV) and $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ (Group II) precipitate with different group reagents. Therefore, the cation present is $\text{Sr}^{2+}$.

Answer: $\text{Sr}^{2+}$
questions.explanation:
The reagent mixture of $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$, $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$, and $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{CO}_3$ is the group reagent for Group V cations in systematic qualitative analysis.

$\text{Zn}^{2+}$ (Group IV) and $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ (Group II) precipitate with different group reagents. Therefore, the cation present is $\text{Sr}^{2+}$.

Answer: $\text{Sr}^{2+}$

questions.q: Which of the following statements regarding the borax bead test of transition metal salts is INCORRECT?
questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding the borax bead test of transition metal salts is INCORRECT?
options: Cobalt salts yield a deep blue bead in both oxidizing and reducing flames.
Chromium salts produce a green bead in both oxidizing and reducing flames.
Copper salts form a blue bead when heated in a reducing flame.
Manganese salts give an amethyst coloured bead in an oxidizing flame and a colourless bead in a reducing flame.
questions.solution:
In the borax bead test, different transition metals form characteristic coloured metaborates depending on the nature of the flame.

Cobalt forms Co(II) metaborate, which is blue in both oxidizing and reducing flames.

Chromium forms Cr(III) metaborate, which is green in both flames.

Manganese forms Mn(II) metaborate, which is amethyst (violet) in an oxidizing flame and colourless in a reducing flame.

Copper forms Cu(II) metaborate in an oxidizing flame, which is blue when cold (and green when hot). However, in a reducing flame, it is reduced to Cu(I) metaborate (colourless when hot) or metallic copper (opaque red when cold). Therefore, copper does not form a blue bead in a reducing flame.

Thus, the statement about copper salts is incorrect.

Answer: Copper salts form a blue bead when heated in a reducing flame.

questions.question: During Lassaigne's test for the detection of sulphur in an organic compound, the sodium fusion extract is treated with sodium nitroprusside. questions.solution:
During Lassaigne's test for sulphur, the sodium fusion extract contains sodium sulphide ($\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{S}$).

When sodium nitroprusside, $\mathrm{Na}_2\left[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_5 \mathrm{NO}\right]$, is added to this extract, it reacts with the sulphide ions to form a deep purple coloured complex.

The chemical reaction is given by:
$\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{S} + \mathrm{Na}_2\left[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_5 \mathrm{NO}\right] \rightarrow \mathrm{Na}_4\left[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_5 \mathrm{NOS}\right]$

Thus, the correct formula of the purple complex is $\mathrm{Na}_4\left[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_5 \mathrm{NOS}\right]$.

To this solution, solid $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ is added followed by an excess of $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$, resulting in the formation of Precipitate A. The mixture is filtered, and $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ gas is passed through the filtrate, which leads to the formation of Precipitate B. The colors of Precipitate A and Precipitate B, respectively, are:
questions.question: An aqueous solution contains a mixture of $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ and $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ ions. To this solution, solid $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ is added followed by an excess of $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$, resulting in the formation of Precipitate A. The mixture is filtered, and $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ gas is passed through the filtrate, which leads to the formation of Precipitate B. The colors of Precipitate A and Precipitate B, respectively, are:
questions.solution:
The separation of cations in qualitative analysis is based on the sequential use of group reagents. The addition of $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ in the presence of $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ is the group reagent for Group III cations.

In the given mixture, $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ belongs to Group III and precipitates as iron(III) hydroxide, $\text{Fe(OH)}_3$. This precipitate has a characteristic reddish-brown color, which identifies Precipitate A.

The filtrate contains the $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ ions, which belong to Group IV. When $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ gas is passed through this alkaline filtrate, manganese(II) precipitates as manganese(II) sulphide, $\text{MnS}$. The characteristic color of $\text{MnS}$ is buff (flesh-colored), which identifies Precipitate B.

Therefore, the colors of Precipitate A and Precipitate B are reddish-brown and buff, respectively.

Answer: Reddish-brown and Buff

questions.q: In the qualitative analysis of Group II cations, hydrogen sulfide ($\mathrm{H_2S}$) gas is passed through the original solution in the presence of dilute hydrochloric acid ($\mathrm{HCl}$). The primary chemical reason for adding dilute $\mathrm{HCl}$ before passing $\mathrm{H_2S}$ gas is to :
questions.question: In the qualitative analysis of Group II cations, hydrogen sulfide ($\mathrm{H_2S}$) gas is passed through the original solution in the presence of dilute hydrochloric acid ($\mathrm{HCl}$). The primary chemical reason for adding dilute $\mathrm{HCl}$ before passing $\mathrm{H_2S}$ gas is to :
options: increase the concentration of $\mathrm{S}^{2-}$ ions for faster precipitation
increase the concentration of $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$ ions to form soluble chloride complexes
dissolve any interfering phosphate ions present in the mixture
decrease the concentration of $\mathrm{S}^{2-}$ ions by common ion effect
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{HCl}$ is a strong acid that completely dissociates to give $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ and $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$ ions.

$\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}^{+} + \mathrm{Cl}^{-}$

Hydrogen sulfide ($\mathrm{H_2S}$) is a weak diprotic acid that ionizes as:

$\mathrm{H_2S} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{H}^{+} + \mathrm{S}^{2-}$

The presence of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ ions from $\mathrm{HCl}$ suppresses the ionization of $\mathrm{H_2S}$ due to the common ion effect. This significantly decreases the concentration of $\mathrm{S}^{2-}$ ions in the solution. The reduced $[\mathrm{S}^{2-}]$ is sufficient to exceed the extremely low solubility product ($K_{\mathrm{sp}}$) of Group II sulfides, but it is too low to precipitate Group IV sulfides, thereby ensuring selective precipitation.

Answer: decrease the concentration of $\mathrm{S}^{2-}$ ions by common ion effect

questions.q: When a metal cation $M^{2+}$ is treated with dimethylglyoxime in an ammoniacal medium, a highly stable bright red precipitate is formed. The hybridization of the central metal atom and the magnetic nature of this precipitate are respectively:
questions.question: When a metal cation $M^{2+}$ is treated with dimethylglyoxime in an ammoniacal medium, a highly stable bright red precipitate is formed. The hybridization of the central metal atom and the magnetic nature of this precipitate are respectively:
questions.solution:
The formation of a bright red precipitate with dimethylglyoxime (DMG) in an ammoniacal medium is a characteristic test for the $Ni^{2+}$ cation. The complex formed is bis(dimethylglyoximato)nickel(II), $[Ni(dmg)_{2}]$.

In this complex, $Ni^{2+}$ has a $3d^{8}$ electronic configuration. DMG acts as a strong field bidentate ligand due to the formation of stable five-membered chelate rings stabilized by intramolecular hydrogen bonding. This strong ligand field forces the pairing of the $3d$ electrons, leaving one $3d$ orbital empty.

Therefore, the hybridization involves one $3d$, one $4s$, and two $4p$ orbitals, resulting in $dsp^{2}$ hybridization (square planar geometry). Since all electrons are paired, the complex is diamagnetic.

Answer: $dsp^{2}$ and diamagnetic

questions.question: An unknown inorganic salt $\mathrm{S}$ is treated with aqueous $\mathrm{NaOH}$ and warmed, evolving a colourless gas $\mathrm{G}$. Gas $\mathrm{G}$ produces a brown precipitate when passed through Nessler's reagent. An aqueous solution of salt $\mathrm{S}$ is treated with dilute $\mathrm{HNO}_3$ followed by $\mathrm{AgNO}_3$ solution, yielding a curdy white precipitate that is completely soluble in an aqueous solution of gas $\mathrm{G}$. The chemical identity of the unknown salt $\mathrm{S}$ is:
questions.solution:
When salt $\mathrm{S}$ is treated with aqueous $\mathrm{NaOH}$ and warmed, a colourless gas $\mathrm{G}$ is evolved which gives a brown precipitate with Nessler's reagent. This confirms that gas $\mathrm{G}$ is ammonia ($\mathrm{NH}_3$) and the salt $\mathrm{S}$ contains the ammonium cation ($\mathrm{NH}_4^+$).

When the aqueous solution of salt $\mathrm{S}$ is treated with dilute $\mathrm{HNO}_3$ and $\mathrm{AgNO}_3$, a curdy white precipitate is formed. This indicates the presence of chloride ions ($\mathrm{Cl}^-$), as silver chloride ($\mathrm{AgCl}$) is a curdy white precipitate.

The precipitate $\mathrm{AgCl}$ is completely soluble in aqueous ammonia (aqueous solution of gas $\mathrm{G}$) due to the formation of the soluble complex $[\mathrm{Ag}(\mathrm{NH}_3)_2]\mathrm{Cl}$.

Therefore, the unknown salt $\mathrm{S}$ is ammonium chloride ($\mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{Cl}$).

Answer: $\mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{Cl}$

questions.q: Two unknown $3d$ transition metal chlorides, Salt A and Salt B, are tested with aqueous potassium ferrocyanide, $\mathrm{K}_4[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6]$. Salt A produces a chocolate brown precipitate, while Salt B produces a Prussian blue precipitate. The spin-only magnetic moments (in BM) of the metal cations present in Salt A and Salt B, respectively, are:
questions.question: Two unknown $3d$ transition metal chlorides, Salt A and Salt B, are tested with aqueous potassium ferrocyanide, $\mathrm{K}_4[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6]$. Salt A produces a chocolate brown precipitate, while Salt B produces a Prussian blue precipitate. The spin-only magnetic moments (in BM) of the metal cations present in Salt A and Salt B, respectively, are:
questions.solution:
The reaction of metal cations with potassium ferrocyanide, $\mathrm{K}_4[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6]$, gives characteristic precipitates.

Salt A forms a chocolate brown precipitate, which indicates the presence of the $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$ ion. The precipitate is cupric ferrocyanide, $\mathrm{Cu}_2[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6]$.
The electronic configuration of $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$ is $[\mathrm{Ar}] 3d^9$. It has $1$ unpaired electron ($n = 1$).
Spin-only magnetic moment $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{1(1+2)} = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.73 \text{ BM}$.

Salt B forms a Prussian blue precipitate, which indicates the presence of the $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ ion. The precipitate is ferric ferrocyanide, $\mathrm{Fe}_4[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6]_3$.
The electronic configuration of $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ is $[\mathrm{Ar}] 3d^5$. It has $5$ unpaired electrons ($n = 5$).
Spin-only magnetic moment $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{5(5+2)} = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.92 \text{ BM}$.

Therefore, the spin-only magnetic moments are $1.73$ and $5.92$ respectively.

Answer: $1.73$ and $5.92$
